discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope built into the Antarctic ice, and turned it into a working instrument. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, opening a new window on the high-energy Universe. The 2017 real-time alert IceCube-170922A, followed up by Fermi and MAGIC, pointed to the blazar TXS 0506+056. This was the first multi-messenger identification of a likely cosmic-ray accelerator, achieved through the same alert culture between physicists and astronomers that made GW170817 possible. IceCube later found neutrino emission from the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022) and mapped the neutrino Galactic plane (2023). Neutrinos are the only messenger that directly traces hadronic acceleration. Halzen's vision created neutrino astronomy and made it a pillar of multi-messenger astrophysics, complementary to gravitational waves and photons.
